CUDA graph replay accelerates execution primarily by eliminating the significant CPU-side overhead associated with launching kernels individually. In eager execution, every kernel launch requires the CPU to validate arguments, manage stream dependencies, and submit commands to the GPU driver, which can take several microseconds per launch. For workloads with many small kernels, this CPU latency often dominates the total execution time, leaving the GPU idle while waiting for instructions. CUDA graphs capture the entire sequence of operations—including kernel launches, memory copies, and synchronization points—into a static directed acyclic graph (DAG) beforehand. When replayed, the GPU executes this pre-compiled graph as a single atomic unit, bypassing the per-launch CPU validation and driver overhead, thereby reducing latency and improving GPU utilization.

However, this performance gain comes with specific costs and constraints. The primary cost is the upfront overhead of capturing and instantiating the graph, which involves recording the execution sequence and optimizing it for the GPU. This makes CUDA graphs less suitable for dynamic workloads where the structure of the computation changes frequently or where kernel parameters vary significantly between iterations, as re-capturing the graph for each change would negate the benefits.
